html:
The regimes that held south and southwest China after the Ming fell in 1644, before the Qing completed their conquest. The map shows them in 1650 and 1700.

In 1650 the southwest was held by the Southern Ming, princes of the Ming house who kept a court in exile. The last of them, the Yongli Emperor, relied on former rebel armies led by generals such as Li Dingguo. The Qing pushed them steadily west. In 1659 Yongli fled to Burma; he was handed over and put to death in 1662. On the coast, the loyalist Koxinga fought on and took Taiwan.

The Qing then left the south to three Chinese generals who had helped them conquer it, the Three Feudatories. The strongest was Wu Sangui in Yunnan. When the Kangxi Emperor moved to abolish their fiefs in 1673, they rose. The Revolt of the Three Feudatories lasted until 1681 and left the south firmly under Qing rule. By 1700 no warlords remained, so the label in that year is a leftover.
sum: The regimes that held south and southwest China after the Ming fell in 1644, before the Qing completed their conquest. The map shows them in 1650 and 1700.
